name: Setting Up an NFS Server
description:
Introduction

NFS (Network File System) allows you to share a directory located on one networked computer with other computers/devices on that network. The computer where directory located is called the server and computers or devices connecting to that server are called clients. Clients usually 'mount' the shared directory to make it a part of their own directory structure.

NFS is perfect for creating NAS (Networked Attached Storage) in Linux/Unix environment. It is a native Linux/Unix protocol as opposed to Samba which uses the SMB protocol developed by Microsoft. The Apple OS has good support for NFS. Windows 7 has some support for NFS.

name: Simple NFS server
description:
First we will Install nfs packages with command like :
yum install nfs*
Now lets create directory which needs to be shared with client machine.
mkdir -p /export && chmod 777 /export
It's important that /export have 777 permissions as we will be accessing the NFS share from the client without LDAP/NIS authentication.

Add /etc/exports entries

To export our directories - in read-write mode- to a local network clients we add the following two lines to /etc/exports
/export       *(rw)
If you want to expose this share to specific client, then replace * with client ipaddress

Portmap Lockdown (optional)

Add the following line to /etc/hosts.deny:
rpcbind mountd nfsd statd lockd rquotad : ALL
By blocking all clients first, only clients in /etc/hosts.allow below will be allowed to access the server. Now add the following line to /etc/hosts.allow:
 rpcbind mountd nfsd statd lockd rquotad : list of IP addresses

Where the "list of IP addresses" string is, you need to make a list of IP addresses that consists of the server and all clients. These have to be IP addresses because of a limitation in portmap (it doesn't like hostnames).

NFS Daemons

NFS serving is taken care of by five daemons: rpc.nfsd, which does most of the work; rpc.lockd and rpc.statd, which handle file locking; rpc.mountd, which handles the initial mount requests, and rpc.rquotad, which handles user file quotas on exported volumes. Most of these programs started during boot-time. If not you may need to start them with command : service rpcbind start In our system they are running . Lets go ahead and restart the NFS server
service nfs start

name: List exported volumes
description:
Just to ensure that NFS Server is running and configured use showmount command.
showmount -e localhost
or find the ipaddress of this machine via ifconfig and use it instead of localhost. 
Export list for 172.31.6.122:
/export *
It displays list of exported NFS shares from the server.

name: NFS client
description:
Lets forget everything for-a-moment and close your eyes ,then imagine you logging into different client machine where you want to access NFS-server :) This is imagination needed because we are using single machine as both Server and Client!.
So now you logged into client machine. You should try and mount "remote" server under specific path. Basic syntax is : 
 mount serverip:/exported_path  /local/mount/path
In our case, we use :
mount localhost:/export /mnt
or via ipaddress of NFS server
mount 172.31.6.122:/export /mnt
will share the remote servers directory locally on /mnt. The df command output shows nfs-mount point. 
# df                                                  
Filesystem           1K-blocks    Used Available Use% Mounted on                
/dev/xvde              8256952 4518116   3319408  58% /                         
tmpfs                   302244       0    302244   0% /dev/shm                  
172.31.6.122:/export   8257024 4518144   3319424  58% /mnt
Now go ahead and create files under /mnt
date > /mnt/f1.txt
they will magically appear on NFS-Server exported volume (/export)
ls /export
You have learned how to install NFS packages and configure then mount it on client machine! That's it for our short NFS How-To. See you later!
